utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, if you're ready, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. Case Number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand? His microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can follow in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Sureta Chana, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you all. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I'm here with Aleksandar Vujic and Cynthia Dresden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you all. I understand that one of the witnesses has a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One of the witness is ill, Your Honour, and is not able to attend. That would be number 48. What we have is number 49.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the consequence of that? He will be heard some other time or you're giving up?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We don't know. We may give up. I won't know for another day or two about his current medical condition. It may be such that he can't even testify in the future. It came as a bit of a surprise to us yesterday, and we haven't had a chance to look into it very much. That's where we are. I have another matter to raise in private session, if we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning again once more, Mr. Talic. Now the members of the public can follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. As I explained to you earlier on, you are about to start giving evidence in this ongoing case against Radoslav Brdjanin. And our Rules require that before you do so, you enter a declaration, a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath that in the course of your testimony, you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. You are -- do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Can I start?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, not yet. When I tell you, please. I appreciate your enthusiasm to give evidence, but you will do it when I tell you. You are going to be handed the text of this solemn declaration now. Please take it in your hand, read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. Now, what's going to happen is that you will first be asked a series of questions by Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Ackerman, I suppose, you have met already. He is the lead counsel for Radoslav Brdjanin --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is the lead counsel for Radoslav Brdjanin. After he's finished with his set of questions, you will then be asked a series of questions in cross-examination by --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Ms. Chana, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- Ms. Chana for the Prosecution. And your duty in terms of the solemn declaration that you have made is to answer all questions truthfully and fully, irrespective of who is putting them to you. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So Mr. Ackerman is going to first with his first question. Mr. Ackerman, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Talic. How are you today?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I'm fine, thank you. How are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Fine, thank you. Would you tell the Chamber when and where you were born, please.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I was born in Celinac on the 20th of April 1940 in Zdravka Celera Street, Celinac, near Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where did you live in the years 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I lived in Celinac up until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Talic, I have a series of questions that I'm going to ask you, and I would request that you listen very carefully to my questions and make sure that you confine your answer to the questions that I --

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is that acceptable to you?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How long have you known Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I have known him ever since he started school in Celinac. He lived with us, that is, in a Muslim house and went to school there. And he was director in Krajina of two companies, Gradjenje and Standard. These two work units were united together, unified into a company called Krajina. He was born some 6 kilometres away from me. I know him very well. I know his family very well. And he knows very well our family, the Talics.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You just told the Chamber that when he went to school in Celinac that he lived with a Muslim family. Do you know the name of that family?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know. Junuz Jusic. He lived with Junuz Jusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You mentioned in an answer a moment ago that he at one point became a director of a company in Celinac. Did you have any association with the company, the Standard company --

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: In Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Did you have any association with that company when he was its director?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was a director of a working unit in Banja Luka, and I worked as a construction worker in Banja Luka. And there were two work units, Gradjenje and Standard. I worked in Standard, and he became the director of the Standard company. The general director was someone else. Well, it was a long time ago, I've forgotten it. But for a while before the war, he was director of Standard. He was my director, therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: During how long a period of time was he the director while you were working there? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I could not tell you precisely, but for a year or two. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you observe during that time whether he treated -- well, let me ask the question differently. Were there other non-Serb employees of Standard at the time? You weren't the only one, were you?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I wasn't the only one, nor did Mr. Brdjanin mind, nor did Muslims themselves mind that. I can tell you on my part that I was very well received and that nobody paid attention to ethnicities. I can tell you that there were quite a few Muslims who worked at Krajina. I can also say that I never felt with Mr. Brdjanin, although I was not on such intimate terms with him so as to sit down with him at a table with him and talk. But before the war broke out, when the war broke out, I sat with him in the office in Celinac, and he actually helped me quite a great deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We'll come to that in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Yes. But what I want to say is the following: I was very well received at -- in Krajina. I had my own brigade and whatever I needed I received. I was -- also appeared in the papers, and Mr. Brdjanin is very well aware of that. And I also am very well familiar with the events surrounding Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I neglected to ask you specifically, although I think it's clear from your testimony, by ethnicity you are a Muslim, aren't you, Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I'm a Muslim, Bosnian. Well, they can call me whatever they want.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Back now to Standard, as the director of Standard, did you ever see any indication that Mr. Brdjanin treated the non-Serb employees any differently from the Serb employees?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've already told us that you were living in Celinac throughout the year 1992. Did there come a time in Celinac in 1992 when the Muslim population became frightened of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were there any -- did the Serb population of Celinac change any during the year 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: As for the Serbs in Celinac, we had no trouble with them. We lived as brethren. I lived in the very centre of Celinac. People knew me very well, and I have never been afraid of the Serbs. We will come to that later. As for 1992, there were no problems up until 1993. It was in 1993 that the unrest began.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a transcript correction. It's page 11, line 17. The witness said that he received some kind of an award from the company that was mentioned in the newspaper. That didn't quite get in the transcript the way he said it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't find it in line 17. It may be different in yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He said: "I was also appeared in the papers," in page 11, line 17. And what he said there was that he had received an award, and that appeared in the papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, I see. Is that correct, Mr. Talic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was an award that wasn't a monetary one. It was -- they just wrote in the papers that I was appreciated as a very good worker, and this constituted a great award for me. But I will tell you later on what sort of an award I was given by Brdjanin and what he did for me. That's something that we will talk about later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of any statements made by Mr. Brdjanin against non-Serb people?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You never heard him make any of those kinds of statements?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Well, I personally didn't hear that. To tell you the truth, there was no electricity. It wasn't possible to watch television so much or listen to the radio. Occasionally we would have that, but specifically that I heard any kind of order from Brdjanin, Brdjanin was a leader, at a leadership position in Celinac, and he only contributed to the calming of the situation. But we will come to that later. He actually established order and discipline in Celinac. So there were no excesses which were unwanted by any ethnic group, and particularly by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I'm trying --

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: That's as much as I want to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- at any time, did anyone tell you that Mr. Brdjanin had made comments, speeches, and so forth that were very derogatory and against Muslim people? Did you ever hear that from any source at all?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything like that, and I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. During the time that you were aware of Mr. Brdjanin being a director at Standard, what kind of a director was he?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Great. We didn't have any extra salary for four or five months. He was -- there was another director who managed the firm badly. And the firm was almost in ruins. It was almost ruined, practically ruined. As soon as Mr. Brdjanin came, we immediately received half of our extra salary. In the third month, we received the second part of the extra salary. And then afterwards, our salaries were very, very good. I know him very well as a construction engineer, designer, as a person, and I never noticed. He knew very well how many Muslims there were in Standard, and everything else. So that man never -- at least, I never heard him make such statements. I know that -- I'm familiar with practically 90 per cent of the kind of conduct of his towards the Muslim population in Celinac. But we'll come to that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: These statements that you just alluded to, again, do you know if any Muslims in Celinac became frightened as a result of hearing Mr. Brdjanin say anything at all?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear from anyone that Brdjanin intimidated Muslims. It's normal that there was fear amongst the people, both Muslims and Serbs and also the Croats when the war began in Bosnia and Herzegovina, when everybody was waging war against everyone else. So it's natural that the situation changed and that the people were frightened. That is true. But as far as hearing anything about Brdjanin, I specifically did not, and I cannot say what is not true and what I did not hear. That's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you just tell the Chamber that all the people in Celinac were frightened, including Serbs? Is that what your position is?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: That's true. That's true. I went to the municipality building --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you this.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we'll come to that in a moment, so let's just wait until we get there. Do you know of your own personal knowledge of any Muslim people or any non-Serb people in Celinac or elsewhere who were hurt in any way by things that Mr. Brdjanin either said or did?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I did not notice anything like that and cannot say anything about that. I am saying again that I never heard Mr. Brdjanin say anything like that, nor did I hear anybody else say that. People know me well in Celinac. I live in the centre of town, about 500 metres away. So in 1992, 1993 all the way up to 1995, I sat with Serbs in cafes in the municipality, and they never looked at me in a weird way, nor did I look at them in any strange way. I never heard of anyone, a Muslim, a Romanie, a Croat, that Brdjanin had said this or that or anything like that. So I never heard anything like that. Later we will come to the specific encounter between Brdjanin and myself at the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to ask you now the other side of the question that I just asked you. In late 1991 or any time in 1992, do you know of any non-Serb persons, any Muslim persons, who were helped in any way by Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Well, I can say that he did help. He would come to the municipal building. People at the municipal building told me that, that he would come and that he would try to calm down the situation to prevent complications from the Serb and Muslim inhabitants, and to continue to live the way we lived before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Chamber has heard about an incident in Celinac where a large number of Muslims were gathered and perhaps even placed on buses. Do you know anything about that situation?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I know very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber what you observed during that incident, where you were, what you observed, what you saw happen?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Listen, if I can say before that something happened, that we had to go to buses, I'm not sure exactly in 1992, there was the encounter between myself and Brdjanin at the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Go ahead and tell the Chamber about the encounter between you and Brdjanin at the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Very well. Before that, I went to the SUP or the MUP building, to the police. My daughter, it was Bajram, that's our Muslim holiday. I went to SUP, to the police, as they know me very well because my daughter happened to be in Kotor Varos for Bajram at a relative's place. And then on the second day of Bajram, Kotor Varos was blocked. And I was asking for a police car and driver, for the police to provide a driver and a car so I could bring my daughter from Kotor Varos. The police commander, because there was a fuel shortage going on, told me, but still they knew who I was and what my situation was, so they did give me a police car, but none of the police drivers wanted to go. So I remembered or I -- that I should go and see Mr. Brdjanin at the municipality. So I was fortunate because that day, Mr. Brdjanin said that he was supposed to go to a meeting in Prnjavor. And since the mosque house in Prijedor was burned, Brdjanin was called to come to Celinac. I met him on the staircase, and I said: "Mr. Brdjanin, I would like to speak to you." And he said: "Yes, very well. Go to the office, I'll be up there in a minute." And I came to the office and we sat down together and we talked about all the problems, about everything. And he asked me: "Talic, what is bothering you?" And I told him what it was. And he said: "Yes, Mr. Brdjanin will help you." At 12.00, maybe 11.30 or 12.00, I'm not sure, the meeting was supposed to be held at the Celinac municipal office. So we went out at 11.30 from his office. At that time, Mile Maksimovic came out. I don't know what he was, chief of the ministry or something. And he said from the door: "Mr. Maksimovic, make me a special permit and secure me a driver and a car so that Meho can be taken. When you make this permit, bring it to my office, I'm bringing a stamp and I will stamp it so that Meho can go and bring his daughter back." And he said: "Very well." Ilija came back and he made the certificate for the driver and the vehicle and he took it to the office. And Rajko Orasanin was the driver of the car. He took me to Kotor Varos, and I went and I brought my daughter back, and I returned, and everything went very well. I found my daughter in Kotor Varos, and I managed to bring her back. So this is what Mr. Brdjanin did for me. Secondly, let me tell you about the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let me interrupt you and ask you a question or two about the other matter first. You said that your daughter was in Kotor Varos for Bajram, and you heard that Kotor Varos was blocked. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you mean by that that she was in a situation where she couldn't come back home?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what was your concern? Why were you concerned about your daughter at that stage? Were you concerned about her safety, or you just wanted her to be back home?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: The Muslims and the Croats up there had already fled. They left Kotor Varos and fled to the woods because they were simply afraid. There was -- there was shooting from the Muslim side. It was Bajram, and they were celebrating up in a village called Ravne. And simply Kotor Varos was blocked. Nobody could enter or leave Kotor Varos. The telephone lines were cut, and I was worried about how to -- how everything will pass and what the situation will turn out to be. So I went to see Mr. Brdjanin, and he helped me out. He gave me a car and a driver. I went to Kotor Varos. The municipal car was stopped at the checkpoint, and they allowed me to go in. I went into Kotor Varos. I found my daughter, and when I found her I returned. So everything passed very well, and everything turned out all right. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell the Chamber about when this happened. It was Bajram of 1992, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: It was Bajram, thereabouts. 1991, at the end of 1991 or in early 1992. I don't remember exactly. It has been ten years since then, 10 to 12 years. So you forget some of that. But this is the situation when Mr. Brdjanin helped me out in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After that was the situation with the buses. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: No. Before we were boarded on to the buses, I personally went to the SUP, and two other cousins of mine who were from the outskirts of Celinac, Mehovci and Basici, Mr. Brdjanin knows those places. The Muslims all gathered in the centre of Celinac because it was safer there, more secure. They were not expelled by anyone, they were not expelled, but they were afraid. Fear was prevalent amongst the people. So we had all gathered in Celinac. 1.860 of us were there in Celinac. So before the buses became to deport us, to drive us anywhere, I don't know, but before that, it happened that two evenings before that, 22 Muslim houses were set on fire. When we saw that, I personally went to SUP, and these two relatives of mine from Mehovci and Basici, we went to the SUP and I told them there "is there any possibility that you can protect us?" And they said: "Mr. Talic, we don't know to do with us, never mind what to do with you. We can just tell you go. We don't want to be responsible for anyone. Anyone can do whatever they decide to do." So the same thing they told me at SUP, they told me at the municipal building as well because everybody knows me there very well. Like I said, I sat in cafes with them. I never had any bad looks from any of them. But the refugees who came from the outside or the Serb population that was leaving their homes were coming towards Banja Luka and Celinac, we were afraid of them because I also was a refugee. I know what it is like to be a refugee, to eat refugee bread and live under a refugee sky. So I went to the SUP to tell them. So when they told us all of this, we all gathered together, us Muslims, and we held a meeting. And we had decided to go towards Banja Luka, and we came to the gas station in Celinac. In the meantime, these hamlets, Radovci, Brezik, and all these other hamlets, everybody from there gathered at the gas station there. There was 1.860 of us Muslims. There were maybe 50 or 60 Croats as well. I don't know the exact number. In the meantime, Dr. Mile Kuzmanovic came to the gas station and took us to the municipal building and to the post office. Not an hour had gone by. Women, children, the elderly, the feeble, and the younger people were located in the municipality, in the offices there, in the basement of the post office and so on. So out of curiosity, I wanted to see what would happen. So in the meantime, I could see a car that came from the direction of Banja Luka. It stopped in front of the municipal building. I was quiet. I heard upstairs in the municipal offices some kind of shouting or a quarrel, and I heard Brdjanin's voice. In the meantime, Gojko Gligoric, I don't know whether he was a corporal or a shift leader, anyway, he was in the army. He wasn't any kind of -- what can I say? He wasn't any kind of important person. But anyway, he picked up the phone in the military point. But any time when he came back from the army, we used to sit down, have a cigarette, we would talk. He would say: "Meho, are there any problems or not?" So then I was quiet, and Gojko literally told me that Mr. Brdjanin said and how some people wanted to blow up the municipal building and the post office and to kill us all. Gojko literally said if it's necessary to kill the Muslims, I will do it myself if they're guilty. And I heard Brdjanin tapped Gojko on the shoulder. And in the morning, Brdjanin ordered that buses come, so the buses came in the morning to take us away. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Brdjanin ordered us to go to the elementary school, to stay there and to be secured properly, to be guarded properly. And this was done. We went to the school. We were guarded. We were protected. Food was brought. Bread, and so on. We weren't hungry or starving for eight days. After eight days, whether this was Brdjanin's order or not I don't know, but we were supposed to go to our houses, all of us, under escort, and all of those who had cattle or poultry, and then also to clean up a little bit, and this is what we did. We went to our homes, and we came back. I don't know how long we were there. For 15 days or something. After that, we were allowed to go to our homes, and we were guaranteed that nothing would happen to us. And this is what happened. That's how it was. I don't know whose order this was, but it's probably Brdjanin's order. And I -- just one second. We went to our homes, and there were no problems. We continued living there, working. Since there were quite a lot of people and since all the inhabitants couldn't receive all of the Muslims who had come from the outside, those from the Vrbanja, Gornji Seher, Vrbas, and so on. So then in 1992 and early 1993, all the younger people, the youth, both boys and girls, young men and women, had already started to leave the territory of Republika Srpska and to go to seek their fortunes outside, in other countries. They organised in Banja Luka. There were these organisations. Of course, you had to pay for transport. They went for sure. I have a son and a daughter, and the same thing happened. They went. They left, and I stayed until 1995, until August 1995. I saw that things were not going to turn out well, that things were brewing, war was going on, money was running out. It was difficult to survive. From the municipality, we asked, we appealed to them. We talked. They sent people. They made a list of those who wanted to leave. They were allowed to leave. They should make a statement that they were leaving, and that is what we did. I was amongst those people also. Since my children had gone to Germany, I have a brother there who has been working in Germany for 40 years. My children went to him. And in 1995, in August, I went to Davor. I crossed into Croatia. I received all sorts of guarantees from my brother, but in Zagreb it was not -- nobody could be received by Germany any more, so I had to stay in Zagreb or in Croatia. My son-in-law lived in my house. He's a Serb. He was living in my house in 1998 when I got in touch with him, and I returned again. He said I could come back, that it was safe. So my wife and I returned, came back to our house without any problems. To this very day, I am living there, I'm working there. I am sick, so I work as much as I can. I am surviving, so to say. When the Serbs don't have work, I don't have work either. This is normal. There's a crisis. So even after I left in 1995, there was still some Muslims who remained in Celinac, and no harm came to them. But this was perhaps up to about 80 Muslims who remained, and that's how it ended, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I have a lot of questions to ask you about some of the things that you said. You talked at one point of being in front of the municipal building, and Mr. Brdjanin had arrived and gone inside, and you said you could hear his voice from inside the building. Do you have any recollection as to what it was you heard him saying?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I couldn't hear exactly what he was saying, but I could just hear him shouting, raising his voice up there to those officials. I heard that personally, that he was shouting at them. This was the second or the third floor. The windows were closed, of course. So it wasn't possible to hear everything that he was saying. But I know very well that he ordered that we should be put in the elementary school and that there should be a guard for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you then made prisoners there in the elementary school? Were you in custody? Were you prisoners, or were you being protected? Which was it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Protected us. Nobody was detained. We could go out. We could walk in front of the municipal building and the post office. It was all close by. We were not detained. We could go out freely. They were really protecting us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have a sense of who among the leadership in Celinac is responsible for you and the 859 other Muslims being protected there at that time? 1.859 is what I meant to say if I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Well, I gave a statement about these three Serbs, but I don't want to mention their names. You have it written there. Do you have them written down there?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You didn't understand my question, sir. My question was: Who do you believe is responsible --

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- for the 1.860 persons in Celinac being protected and placed in the school and being protected? Who do you think is responsible for that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin. And three other Serbs who reported to the military police. When we wanted to go to Banja Luka, they informed the military police, these three Serbs - two of them are still alive; one of them is dead - but I wouldn't want them to have any consequences, because of their neighbours, people are people. There are extremists on all sides, and there will still be such people. So if it's not necessary, I wouldn't want to mention their names, but I can do that. So they reported to the military police. They were in Kotor Varos. They came, they stopped us. In the meantime, as I said, Mile Kuzmanovic, the doctor, came and returned us to the municipal building, and after that Brdjanin was called for sure because he came, he had heard about it. So I give recognition for this, the most to Mr. Brdjanin. He personally saved the Muslim population. It was him personally. I stand by this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told the Chamber that in 1992 that several of the young people, and the words you used were "they left to seek their fortunes elsewhere." My question is were these young people forced to leave, or did they leave of their own free will?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: They left of their own free will.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you left, were you forced to leave or did you leave of your own free will?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Of my own will. No one forced me to, no one. We were merely protected. There were two people from the municipality building who made a list of those who wanted to leave, and those were to be escorted. And those who didn't want to could remain. I told my children, son and daughter, that they should leave as well. I told them: "You have the papers. Leave. You will inherit this world." And as for us, the older ones, we'll see what the situation will be like. And that is how it happened. I sent my two children away. They were in no way forced to leave. I ordered them to leave Celinac. There were many parents who had such young children who asked them to leave the territory of Republika Srpska. They did not even go to the federation. Many of them went abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Talic. That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Chana, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Talic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may remain seated if you prefer.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Talic. Mr. Talic, are you hearing me?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Talic, do you hear me? Good morning, Mr. Talic.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I hear you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I hear you well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: -- please, you said you worked with Mr. Brdjanin in this factory called Krajina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you know a factory called -- a workshop called 25th November?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: This was a company in Celinac, a construction company.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Wasn't that the company that Mr. Brdjanin also worked in?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before arriving to Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But you worked with him in the Krajina company?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I started working with Krajina before him. He started working there later on when he came to Celinac. There was also the 25th November, the construction company in Celinac which had suffered severe losses. Mr. Brdjanin then came to work for it and managed to pull it out of the crisis. And when he did so, I heard from some people that he had some trouble with the people -- with his associates working in the company. Mr. Brdjanin is a good man, educated man, a very sensible man. Krajina felt this, and that is why Krajina decided to employ him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Talic, thank you very much, but I'd be grateful if you would confine yourself to answering my questions, please. Have you been in touch with Mr. Brdjanin since he has been arrested?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Have you been in touch with any of his family members?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And why is that, Mr. Talic?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I had my personal problems with my health condition. I had to go to the hospital. And it is my health condition that prevented me from keeping in touch with his family, and that is the only reason. I was admitted to the hospital. I suffered severe haemorrhage. I had a heart attack. My liver is a very feeble one. I have a number of diseases that I suffer from. I would have liked to have come to The Hague directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Talic, you said that you were very good friends, family friends with the family and Mr. Brdjanin; and yet, after Mr. Brdjanin was arrested, you had no contact whatsoever with his family. Is that your position, Mr. Talic?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I do not know Mr. Brdjanin's family, nor have I ever spent any time with them. I was only in touch with Mr. Brdjanin. As I have told you, this took place in the municipality building in Celinac. I know Mr. Brdjanin very well, and I know how he behaved in the company and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Where was it that you would meet Mr. Brdjanin that you know him so well?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I knew him because I used to see him in the company, and I specifically met with him in the municipal assembly of Celinac. I sat there with him for two hours. We talked about all sorts of things. And I did not notice that he had anything against Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You just told the Court in your examination-in-chief, Mr. Talic, that you're familiar with 90 per cent of Mr. Brdjanin's conduct. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: 90 per cent of his conduct in the Municipal Assembly of Celinac where he tried to protect us as people. He was guarding us there, making sure nothing bad would happen to us. I guarantee that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Talic, yet you also told this Court that you've not heard any of Mr. Brdjanin's public speeches. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You never listened to the TV?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I've told you a moment ago that there was not much electricity during the war. Secondly, I had my work obligation, and I spent very little time at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Talic, did you listen to the radio at all?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: There was no electricity. And I was constantly carrying out my work obligation. And if I was not carrying out my work obligation at Orasje, I was in Celinac. Maybe only some three hours a day. But there was not much electricity for anyone, not for Serbs or Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were you aware, Mr. Talic, that Mr. Brdjanin did, in fact, make many anti-Muslim comments utterances in his public speeches including calling Muslims balijas and non-Christian scum?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Are you aware now that he made such utterances, or are you still blissfully unaware?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I know nothing of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You said that you were very familiar with everything which was happening in Celinac Municipality. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And you obviously know that Celinac was a Serb-dominated municipality?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: As a municipality, the predominant population was the Serb one. Now, the centre is a small town of Celinac where 80 per cent.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction, 90 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Was Muslim populated. However, when you look at the entire territory of the municipality, that's where the Serb population was predominant.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Would it be true to say that there were no more than 1.440 Muslims in the entire municipality?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: 1.860 in the entire territory of Celinac Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And would it also be true to say that by the end of 1995, 190 Muslims remained in this municipality?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: In August 1995, there were three buses having 60 passengers each, meaning 180 of us, who were headed on these buses for Croatia. And maybe some 50 to 80 Muslims remained there throughout this time who never left Celinac. They didn't want to go. These were Muslims. And they were not driven away by Serbs. They remained there and didn't experience any trouble. And that is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So Mr. Talic, the truth -- the fact of the matter is most of the Muslims did leave the municipality, and I'll come to in a minute as to why they left.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You said all the people in the municipality were frightened, which included Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What were the Serbs frightened of?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: The Serbs were frightened, as far as I know -- that is, I know that they were frightened because I visited some of the families that I was friends with. And we had our bags packed in our home, and so did the Serbs. And when the war broke out and when there was a threat of the Serbs' positions being shelled, well, as far as I understand, this is what they were afraid of. It doesn't have to be necessarily true, but I am convinced that that is where their fears lay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But the Serbs did not leave the municipality, did they, Mr. Talic?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: No, nor were the positions around Banja Luka bombed, nor were there any war operations going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Talic, in early April 1992, May 1992, were there not severe economic and social restrictions placed on the Muslim population of Celinac Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were not any restrictions. The Muslims, that is, we, the elderly people, or maybe some people five years my junior, we did not go out into the centre of Celinac, to the shops. Well, we were afraid of drunkards, some of those knew us, and we would actually send women to the shops instead. Many people knew our wives, and our wives would go to the shops to buy whatever was necessary. And my wife, for instance, would always go whenever we needed something. And she was told by Serb sales ladies and salesmen "why isn't Meho coming to shop? Nothing will happen to him." That is what they told everyone. But to be frank, we were afraid of the drunkards, and then there were Serb refugees, and they were afraid of them as well. But I was never afraid of the local Serbs, nor am I afraid today. I told you I was the first one to return. I've had no problems. My son has returned and is visiting cafes and is not encountering any problems. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, page 30, line 8, I'm told the witness said in answer to the last question or part answer to the last question: "When there was threats from NATO, we were both scared, Serbs and Muslims." I think that's what he said. We can check with him if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose, Mr. Talic, you need to confirm that to us. Did you mention NATO at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Let's proceed, Ms. Chana, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. But could I have the usher to bring out P450 so it will be available to me when I come to it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Talic, in April or May 1992, did you hear that the Bosnian Serb authorities broadcast instructions on the radio requiring all Muslims in Celinac to surrender any weapons in their possession? And this was supposed to be done to the crisis staff by 10 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: This isn't correct. Not the crisis staff, but the SUP in Celinac. I was among those who had weapons, and I had the proper license for it. And when the order was issued for the weapons to be surrendered to the SUP, that is what we did, and we surrendered them. And now that you're mentions weapons, I returned in February 1998, and some two or three months later the chief of the SUP told me "Meho, did you submit the request for the return of the weapons?" And I told "no, I haven't, but I will." And he told me: "Well, you should do it in good time because very soon we will start returning weapons." And this is how it went. I was first among the Muslims to be returned my weapons when such time came. And now I have weapons with the proper documentation, and I have no trouble about it from the police, the SUP, or anyone else. I am a legal owner of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Talic, why were only the Muslims required to submit their weapons and not the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Talic, do you also remember - and I want to show you P450 - that on 23rd July 1992, the war presidency of Celinac issued a resolution on the status of the non-Serb population on the territory of the Municipality of Celinac. Do you know anything about this particular resolution before we show it to you? It's now on the ELMO, Mr. Talic. Can you see it now? Do you see this document on the ELMO, Mr. Talic?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: There are some names at the front there. Do you know any of these people who are named under Article 2?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I know all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And they are forbidden -- these are the people -- do you want some time to read the second page of this document? Perhaps page 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: The witness hasn't seen the document before, so perhaps he ought to have a bit of time to look at it before I can question him on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before, Mr. Talic? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You have seen it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I've seen both of them. And read them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: When was it that you first saw this document, Mr. Talic?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: As soon as they were typed out, maybe some 15 days later, I had them in my hands. I personally. May I continue with my answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: The first and last names of these young men contained in this list here, all these are educated people, graduates of universities, young men of repute. There were engineers among them, people of different profiles, occupations.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Now, what the reason was for them being unwanted in Celinac, this is something I could not find out. Simply this list said that they were unwanted in Celinac and that nobody wanted them to move around in Celinac. Secondly, this other document that was written, that Muslims and Croats were forbidden to swim in the Vrbas River, this is true. This document was indeed issued. Now, who ordered that these documents be typed out is something I never found out, although I did try. I did not find out, and even today I do not know who ordered and who typed these documents out. I am constantly in touch with the officials in the municipality, in the SUP and elsewhere, but I have never been able to find out who was it who issued the order and who typed the documents. The truth is that they were, indeed, written and made public.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Talic, you are somebody who knows quite a lot what happened. Can you not give us, suggest any reason as to why these restrictions should have been placed on these individuals? Why do you think this was so?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I have no idea. The only thing I can say is that the persons involved were young, educated, graduates of universities, medical workers. All of them were educated, all those contained on this list. Now, why this was so? Who ordered or typed it out?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Talic, the -- you said the Muslims left Celinac Municipality because they were in fear. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Correct. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What was this fear about? What was it based on?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: First, let me tell you, there were intimidations going on. Fire -- 24 houses were set on fire. Mosques were blown up.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Who set those houses on fire and who blew up these mosques?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: How should I know? One wasn't allowed to go out in the evening. We would gather in larger groups and would hide in safer places, basements, houses of stronger structure. We did not dare to go out and see what was going on because we were afraid of what might happen. Therefore, I do not know who was it who demolished these structures, who set fire to them. I only know that it was terrible. And as I've said, where there was a house, where a hodza would have his liturgy, this house would be blown up. And that's why Mr. Brdjanin had to make this intervention in Celinac, and that's why he went there. And on that day I talked to him, and that day I told you he helped me get my daughter back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise you, Mr. Ackerman, at some point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was just concerned that there's no date being established for these events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Talic, perhaps you could be more specific as regards to the date especially since you now sort of put in one vast category the burning down of houses and blowing up of mosques together with your visit, Mr. Talic, to help you recover your daughter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not recall the date. But this indeed did happen. All these houses were -- are now repaired, reconstructed through donations, international donations. Only perhaps three or four houses still need to be repaired. All the rest have all been repaired. And life goes on without any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How many Muslims have returned to Celinac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, approximately some 200 to 300 persons, mostly elderly ones. And among them, some perhaps 20 younger men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Chana. Sorry for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That's all right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- Break.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I was wondering if it was the appropriate time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Talic, we are going to have a short coffee break now, which will also give you a rest. We will reconvene in 25 minutes' time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Talic, we are going to proceed. Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Talic, you said there were some meetings which were conducted by the SDS of the Serb leadership with the Muslims in the Celinac Municipality. Were you present at any of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Which one were you present at?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I did not attend any meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you know about the meeting which took place in Popovac, the village of Popovac? This was before July sometime, before this document that I showed you was released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you sure about the pronunciation, Ms. Chana? If necessary, we'll spell it for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Popovac. Yes, P-o-p-o-v-a-c.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to make sure that he gets the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct, Popovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you recall about this meeting at all and the incident which happened thereafter?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: No, I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the murders of the Sugic brothers -- by the Sugic brothers?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I heard of that case, yes. Is when you're linking the Sugic's with that, then our Muslims, our young men, went to Popovac or Mehovci, up there, to cut wheat with combine machinery and also with trucks so that the wheat could be cut, put on the trucks, and brought to the warehouse in Popovac. And my son was also there who drove a tractor and the wheat to Popovac. So when all of that was finished, that was true. When they were going from Popovac towards Celinac, the Sugic's came out with weapons, with automatic rifles and machine-guns. I don't know exactly what weapons they had. And 32 of our men were taking the wheat to the mill to be ground so that the soldiers would have food. I'm not sure exactly what the wheat was intended for. Then the Sugic's came out. They set up a barrier and were holding their weapons at the ready. The driver stopped. A police officer came out, Mladen Vrhovac, and two or three other Serbs came out, and they literally said: "Sugic, you can leave so that we can kill the balijas." They said: "No way. While we're there, not a hair on the Muslims' heads can be harmed." And this is what happened. I don't know how long this whole thing lasted, these arguments and everything. And then when they saw that nothing will come of it, that they cannot do what they were intending to do, they withdrew. Our young men came to Celinac. They came back to Celinac alive and well so that everything in the end was okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Talic, I'm talking about the incident where the Sugic brothers murdered the Muslims, the Muslim representatives at this meeting, and they were shot and murdered after this beating. You're talking about another incident, Mr. Talic. And you do recall this particular incident. You heard about it, as did everybody else. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I did hear that this happened in Popovac, but I don't know which Muslim was actually killed. I did hear about this incident. I know the Sugics. I know them well because Mr. Brdjanin knows this cafe in Popovac belonging to the Sugic's where I also worked. So I know them very well. And the Muslim who was killed, I don't really know his name, but I heard that a Muslim was killed in Mehovci or up there in Popovac. I was talking about the Sugics. When we started to talk about them, I was just saying how they were there when there was talk about the killing of our young men, when they were coming back from Popovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So you said that they were calling the Muslims balijas. Is that correct, the Sugic brothers?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And yet, you worked for them?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: We were working for the army. The grain was placed in the military warehouse. That was it. That was this incident, the only one incident that happened with us Muslims in that time. Even those I was on work duty and I was at Orasje on a couple of occasions. That's where the Serb army was as well, people knew me. They invited me for coffee, some plum brandy. There were no excesses there, no incidents. I went to Orasje twice. I was the eldest amongst them. My people said I had to go to the work obligation. They didn't want to go without me. At the municipal office, they said: "Meho, come, you have to go, at least a couple of times so there were no problems." And I did go on a couple of occasions even though people protected me because I was the oldest one. So I also worked with the Serb population. I wasn't imposed any kind of quota, how much I had to do. I did a little bit of work. I worked in the garden and so on. There was no coercion. I wasn't mistreated or abused, not just me but many others. I never went by myself. Other people would go with me also. All in all, it was okay, and it ended well for me and for many of our Muslims. So, well, what can you say?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Talic, you would agree with me that this murder of the Muslim representative after that meeting created a great deal of fear amongst the Muslim population, fear for their safety?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Yes. When this happened, the whole of Mehovci and Basici, their population left that entire area. Mr. Brdjanin knows. This is from that area where he came from, those Muslims. Of course they were frightened, they went down to Kamenovac between Jajce and Banja Luka. And they were in a school at school in Kamenovac for a night or two, and then they were transferred to Celinac to a safer place.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were you aware there was another meeting held by the SDS Bosnian Serb leadership where Brdjanin was present after this particular document was published?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I personally don't know about that meeting. To tell you the truth, I don't know about the meeting, nor do I know that Mr. Brdjanin was present. I told you I was at Orasje on work obligation and that I had also gone to Banja Luka because I had a brother who was ill. So I worked for a Serb refugee who lived in my brother's house. He exchanged a house with a Croat from Bihac, and he was a judge in Banja Luka. And I went to repair his mother and father's house. I had a brother who was mentally ill. He didn't know about the war. He used to smoke four or five packs of cigarettes a day, and there was a crisis with cigarettes, so thanks to this Rada, she obtained cigarettes for me and gave me money. I didn't work for free. I also did some other private jobs in order to survive. And about those meetings, to tell you the truth, I don't really know about them. I don't know whether Mr. Brdjanin was present or not. I know that meetings were held at the municipality, but who held these meetings I don't know. I personally know. I have a friend -- actually, it's a friend of my son's, a Serb, who was in the military police. When the meetings were being held in the municipal building and the Muslim families were being discussed and when I was discussed and my family was discussed, he literally told me - this is a great man - and he said that no harm can come to Talic's family. At that point, my children still had not left. He would come at midnight or at 1.00 in the night, he would knock in the door. There was no telephone, there was no electricity. I recognised his voice. We let him into the house. And he conveyed to us, he said: "Meho, do not be afraid. No harm can come to your family." And not only this person. I can tell you the names of 20 or 30 names of prominent people, honest people, Serbs who used to come at 1.00 at night, knock on the door. They would open their wallet and say "Meho, how much money do you need? Buy yourself bread, flour, whatever food you need. We will bring it to you. We are coming at this time of night so that other Serbs will not attack us" and things like that. I had a brother in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Germany who had been working there for 40 years. Through a Serb who was working there, he would send money to me and I didn't --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Talic, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but matters would be much clearer for everyone if you just answered the questions in some brevity. When you're talking about all of this, when are you talking that this happened? What time frame are you talking about now?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you: Meetings were held on several occasions. I heard about that. But like I said, like I told you before, I didn't spend a lot of time at Celinac. I was either in Banja Luka or at Orasje or on work obligation. So at that time, I wasn't really that much in contact with the Serbs, with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one moment. I'll try to intervene a little bit because we are getting nowhere here.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Talic, these events that you're talking -- telling us about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- these meetings, first of all, let's start with the meetings, are you talking about 1991, 1992, 1993? Can you help us a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The meetings were held in 1991 and 1992 and 1993 as well as in 1994. There were always meetings, accords, but I don't know what kind of meetings they were and what happened. I don't know that. But they were held, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But only during one year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And these Serbs coming to knock at your door at 1.00 or 2.00 in the morning offering you money, are we talking of 1991, 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't understand the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't hear any answer at all. Mr. Talic, in case my question did not get to you, you mentioned Serbs coming to knock at your door at night offering you money, offering you their help. Did this happen in 1991 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whatever I needed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992 and 1993, those two years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. Thank you. Do you need to place any other event, Ms. Chana, in a specific time frame?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I wanted to talk about this particular meeting in about July 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's already said he doesn't know anything about this particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I don't know why we need to pursue it. He's already said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maybe if he's asked a further question, he will suddenly remember what the meeting was. Let's see. If we don't get there, Mr. Ackerman, I will stop Ms. Chana and we will move to some other area.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: At this meeting there were representatives of the Muslim community who would go as representatives and then give the information to all the other Muslims. That was the purpose of this particular meeting. Did you hear the outcome of some of the -- what was discussed at these meetings by the Muslim representatives and the SDS?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: SDS or SDA?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: With the SDS representatives with the Bosnian Serb representatives with the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: She has said a meeting in 1992, and she has now said meetings. So what are we talking about? What question is being asked? And I think first of all it must be established whether he knows about the particular meeting that she wants to ask him about or not. If he doesn't know about it, then there's no sense asking him about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right, Mr. Ackerman. Perhaps we can tackle it from another angle. Please ask him first whether it was customary, whether it was usual for representatives of the Muslims to report back to the Muslim community the outcome of any meetings, of meetings with the Serb representatives. Let's start from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That was my exact point.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Talic, was it customary for the Muslim representatives to give the outcome of the meetings to the general Muslim population of Celinac Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Listen, I remember one of those meetings now. I've remembered it. There were two Muslims who attended it. And I found that out from the Serb population, which two Muslims attended that meeting and who knew what happened at the meeting. Then, those two Muslims did not convey to the Muslim population the situation as it was. So those two same Muslims were looking after their own affairs. I was following them. I kept my eye on them. They were suspicious. So after that meeting, they didn't stay in Celinac for long. They left Celinac. They left and went away. Therefore, we, the other Muslims, did not know at all what was going on that much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Talic, but the question was, was it customary - I will come -- leaving aside this one particular meeting that you now remember about - for the information to be disseminated between the Muslim population. That was the purpose of the meeting, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it was not conveyed to us, or we were not told about it. I didn't hear anything about it. I am saying that I didn't hear anything about it and can say nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Mr. Brdjanin say at one of these meetings that Celinac was for the Serbs and the Muslims must leave?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, is there any factual basis for that question or did she just make up that? Because I don't think there's any basis for that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry I don't normally interrupt like this. But obviously Ms. Chana's -- this is taken from someone who testified, and the page number I think Ms. Chana has got there so we can give the page number of the transcript for Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think what Mr. Ackerman needed to know --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm satisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to make sure that Mr. Talic remembers the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Talic, did you ever hear that at one of these meetings Mr. Brdjanin had told the Muslim representatives that Celinac was for the Serbs and all the Muslims must leave?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I'm claiming 100 per cent that I did not hear that from the Muslims or from the Serbs. And even though I'm 100 per cent convinced, according to my understanding, that Brdjanin would not say that, still I don't know but I doubt that he said that. This could be something that was just fabricated. I just wanted to say three or four words briefly. Just as my Muslims in Celinac don't like me, I can tell you that sincerely. 40 to 50 per cent, even though I'm equal towards everybody and I have everybody in my family, I only judge people if they're good or bad. The same applies to Mr. Brdjanin. He has friends and enemies, Serbs. So I really doubt whether Mr. Brdjanin could have said that. There are opponents of Brdjanin, Serbs, who will also not like the fact or hold it against me that I was a witness and that I came to testify. But I am saying 100 per cent that Brdjanin did not say that because there are people who don't like Brdjanin, and I'm speaking to them openly, and they tell me "we don't like Brdjanin." There are a lot of Serbs there at leadership positions whom Serbs don't like. Let's take Dodik for example. 50 per cent of people of Banja Luka don't like him. So for Mr. Brdjanin also, there are fabrications. I'm a citizen of Celinac. I lived a hundred metres away from the municipal building, so I know how everybody breathes. So I'm surprised that Mr. Brdjanin said that. And if -- I don't know if I am right or not, but I did not hear that. I'm definitely saying that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Talic, since you know how everybody breathes, perhaps you can assist the Court with Mr. Brdjanin's relationship with the Sugic brothers. Were they good friends?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about the relationship between the two -- the three of them, what they were like, whether they were on good terms or not. I cannot say. I don't know. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Would Mr. Brdjanin go to the cafe owned by the Sugic brothers?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I don't like this. Earlier on, and this is one question that I was going to put to you myself, when you mentioned that the Sugic brothers had a cafe, you also indicated that Mr. Brdjanin knew this very well and that he had -- that he frequented this cafe, apart from you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I apologise. I did not say that Mr. Brdjanin went to that cafe. I said Mr. Brdjanin knows about the cafe of the Sugic's in Popovac, the one owned by the sons of Savo Sugic. He has sons - Savo - who was killed. And I know that Mr. Brdjanin knew about that cafe where I used to work. A long time ago when they were just building it, I worked on it and I finished it. I said that Mr. Brdjanin knew about that cafe, but I did not say that he used to go there and he used to have meetings there. No, that is not correct. And one thing 100 per cent, that cafe is 8 kilometres away from my house, so I don't know what was going on, what were the meetings there, who met who there. Because in the centre of Celinac, I don't know what they did at those meetings, what were the words, how the policy was conducted, what was done. I only know that when I was on the agenda and my family, I didn't have any problems, and I will not have any problems. Mr. Brdjanin told me personally when I sat down with him, as soon as I introduced myself and said who I was, he said "you Talics were never extremists, and I don't think that you are now." Neither me nor my family were never like that. As far as I'm concerned, everybody is just a person to me. And people have to be responsible for who they are and for what they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, page 38, line 10, what the witness actually said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know, I have it front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is not what you suggested. He didn't ever say that Brdjanin went to the cafe. He said he knows this cafe and Popovac belonging to the Sugics where I also worked. And that's all he said about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And he said, "I know them well because Mr. Brdjanin knows this cafe in Popovac belonging to the Sugics where I also worked." So let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Talic, you told the Court earlier on, and it's a direct quote from you when you were asked about the Sugic brothers. You said "I know them well because Brdjanin knows this cafe." That is what you've told the Court earlier. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What did you mean to say when you said Mr. Brdjanin knows this cafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that Brdjanin was born in that area, from Popovac. He was born up there and that he was educated in Celinac and Banja Luka. I don't know where he finished his university education, but Mr. Brdjanin is from that area. And even if he weren't, he should have known each family in Celinac, in the Celinac Municipality, because he was in a leadership position there. And he was born up there. He knew Mehovci, which is a Muslim village, Basici also is a Muslim village, Stasi, Popovac, Lipovac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Talic, please try to be concise in your answer because you are running literally beyond what is being asked of you. My question was a very simple one. You didn't say Mr. Brdjanin knows about the existence of this cafe. You said Mr. Brdjanin knows this cafe, which to me means he's familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everybody from Celinac knows about that cafe, a Muslim -- Muslims and Serbs. There's a bus line running there, a bus stops there. Popovac, Celinac, Sahinovic, and further on. People go up there. People know about that cafe. It's a cafe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Brdjanin's various official -- what he was an official of in the ARK region? Do you know all the posts that he held?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you know that he was the vice-president of the association of municipalities of the Bosnian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I heard something about it, but I don't really know all the details.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you know he was the president of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That will be all from this witness, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Chana. Is there re-examination, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have two or three questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Talic, you talked about the young people leaving, young Muslim people leaving Celinac in 1992. Just so we're all clear, when did the bulk of the Muslim people who left Celinac, what year was it that they actually left?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you briefly. It all depended on the opening of the points in Bosanska Gradiska and the opening up of the crossing over of the crossing over of the Sava River because that was the way out of Republika Srpska. Bosanska Gradiska and Travnik, up there in the direction of Vlasic, those were the two routes. There were organisations in Banja Luka that had their own buses, and you had to pay for the transport. Sometimes the points in Gradiska and Travnik were closed and when they could not receive refugees, and then it took some time so that every year from 1992 up until 1995 people were leaving according to their abilities and the actual possibilities. Sometimes -- well, so they left gradually, not all at once. Sometimes two, three, five buses would leave depending on how many passengers there were, how many passengers -- how many people Croatia could receive and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. That's good enough. Thank you. You mentioned at one point that before there was any -- there were any departure of Muslims from Celinac that the population of the city centre had a certain percentage of Muslims. And it's unclear whether you said 80 per cent or 90 per cent. Because at one time it was reported as 80 per cent, and then it was corrected at 90 per cent. And I'd just like to know which one it was that you actually said.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: 90 per cent were Muslims in the centre of Celinac. And 10 per cent in the very centre of Celinac, which was a small town, were Serbs, 10 or 15 per cent. And as taken as a municipality, Celinac numbered -- actually 90 per cent of the entire population in the municipality were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about the Sugic brothers who were accused of committing these killings that you have been asked about. Were they -- the Sugic brothers, were they the sons of Savo Sugic or were they the sons of Mica Sugic?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Listen, to tell you the truth, I know all these Sugics well. Now, which ones took place in -- were involved in the murders, I don't know. Talking specifically of Savo Sugic, he has two sons. One of them is a driver in Kip in Celinac, and he wouldn't harm an ant. The other brother who resides in Popovac and runs this cafe, I think that this young man is also a very peaceful one. Now, who took -- who took part in these murders, I do not know. That's that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Talic, because I don't know what kind of interpretation you are receiving over there, but to my knowledge it should be perfect. It should be good, like it has always been. You certainly haven't answered Mr. Talic's question -- Mr. Ackerman's question.
