Mr. Ackerman wants to know who these Sugic brothers are that you were talking about. Were they the sons of Savo Sugic or of Mica Sugic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you, there are three or four families of Sugics, and I do not know who participated there, but I do know that the Savo Sugic's junior son who's up there in Popovac, as far as I know, he took no part in that. But specifically, I do not know who took part in the murders. I only heard that there were some Sugics involved in the murders. I cannot tell you which ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's better. Okay. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How many people were living in Popovac in 1992 roughly? Did you hear my question?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How many people were living in Popovac in 1992 roughly, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How many cafes are there in Popovac?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I know for this one cafe, Sugic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know if there are any others?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Talic. That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And before I ask Judge Janu and Judge Taya if they have any questions, just to have it clear in my mind, these Sugics that own this cafe in Popovac, they are the sons of Savo, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Janu from the Czech Republic will be asking you one question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Mr. Talic, do you know why -- the reason why Mr. Brdjanin made enemies among the Serbs? Do you know the reason?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Janu. Judge Taya, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Taya from Japan also has some questions for you, Mr. Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: You said that your son-in-law is a Serb. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have all ethnicities in my family, all sorts of ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Apart from him, do you have any Serb ethnicity person in your close relatives?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I have. My brother's son who married a Serb, we have very friendly terms with them. They have a family of their own now. And then from -- on my cousin's side, I have a cousin married to a Serb also on good terms. My daughter is married to a German. I have a son-in-law who's Albanian. I only don't have a gypsy in my family. And I'm on good terms with everyone. Everyone is treating me well, and I treat them well as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: You are now living in Celinac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: I think you are living together with some persons. Together with whom are you living?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I have a wife and a son who returned from Germany, who is single, and when they were returning the refugees, he was among the first ones to be returned. I work occasionally. I still have to qualify for pension. I do not qualify yet. Now, we have no trouble. We continue living. If there's work to be done, both with Muslims or with Serbs, regardless of who invites us to work, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Where have you been living after 1995 when you left Celinac?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I stayed in Croatia for three years, and then I returned in February 1998 when my son-in-law informed me that I could return. I found an apartment in Croatia, and I paid the rent for it because I didn't want to go to those collection centres. As soon as I crossed the Sava River into Croatia, I went to Oriovac near Slavonski Brod. Found an apartment, paid for it myself, worked a bit, and I lived there. I didn't go back to Sana canton where Muslims would go, where Serbs had abandoned their houses who had left Sanski Most, Bihac. That's where Muslims would go to live. I didn't want to go there. I lived on my own. And then as I came in touch with my son-in-law and he told me I could return, I did, and I have been living in my house to this very day, that much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: How do you make a living nowadays?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: Well, I live from today to tomorrow. I work very little. I am now of -- a bit old, so I have -- my wife works, my son, and then I have some land to work on, and I also work for whoever calls me to work. And that's how I survive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Taya. I have just one question for you, Mr. Talic. And I'm just wondering how you came to know with such detail what was happening in Kotor Varos before you decided to ask for Mr. Brdjanin's help.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: I came to know about it when I made a call because at the time the phone lines were functioning. And when I was trying to reach Kotor Varos, I was unable to reach them there. I had neighbours who also had relatives up there, perhaps whose children married with someone from there and went over there to celebrate Bajram because there it was a bit more peaceful than here. And the town was blocked, the phone lines were cut off. I went to the municipality building, and there they told me that indeed the town was blocked. My daughter happened to be there, and my wife was very angry with me because she told me "you sent her over there. Now you bring her back." She was crying. She was very distressed. So I went wherever I could, and I'm thankful to the Lord, and I wish to thank Mr. Brdjanin who understood my situation, provided me with a car, provided me with a driver and with a special permission, permit, which enabled me to bring my daughter over to Celinac. I crossed a Serbian checkpoint in Kotor Varos, and they allowed me to go through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Talic, because you are repeating yourself. What I wanted to know is this: The town was blockaded. The telephone lines were cut, interrupted. And still, you had so much information. Earlier on, you even told us who was firing, who was shooting, and where the people were hiding or where they had gathered together. I mean, where did you get this information from? You seem to have been very well informed in spite of the fact that the telephone lines were not available, were cut at the time.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TALIC
utterances.text: First, I was told by the Serbs in the municipality building and in the police. I got the information, and then Mr. Brdjanin gave me the car, and I went up there. I came across a checkpoint. There was a lieutenant colonel, or a colonel, a Serb, who told me that Serbs and Muslims were fighting, but then he saw that it was a Serb driving the car and that I was given the permission by a Serb. And he said: "Well, we are fighting Muslims and here it is we have a Muslim in the car." And then they understood that I was on friendly terms with Mr. Brdjanin. I was allowed to go on foot. I had to leave the car on the checkpoint. There was a fire-fighting car there. At the same time, there was an announcement saying that Croats and Muslims had to surrender their weapons and that nobody would harm them, that their security would be guaranteed. I entered Kotor Varos and went to my relatives' house where my daughter was. I found the door locked, and I went into a side street where I met up with a Muslim. He asked me "what do you need, sir, here?" And I said my daughter arrived here some two days ago. And he told me "they're all down there in the woods hiding." I went there, found my daughter, brought her back to the car, and that's how I was aware of what was going on in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That brings your testimony to an end, Mr. Talic. I thank you for having gone over to the offices from where you have given testimony, and I thank you on behalf of the Tribunal and of everyone present here. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I put a question to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to greet you all and would like to greet Mr. Brdjanin. He knows me well. I have the very best wishes for him and wish him to return as soon as possible. I wish to say that Mr. Brdjanin is not -- doesn't have the responsibility that has been attributed to him. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Talic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good-bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ackerman will do his best to try and please Mr. Talic, Mr. Brdjanin, make Mr. Talic happy. Is there any other further business that you would like to -- nothing? I see you both standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I got up first, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As far as the Prosecution is concerned, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so I don't forget later, I'd be very remiss if I didn't express the gratitude of our team, the Brdjanin Defence, for the stellar work of the interpreters throughout this entire trial and the things they did above and beyond the call of duty at times for us was -- we're very appreciative of. And it's our observation that even though we occasionally brought attention to mistranslations, the bulk of the work they did was absolutely flawless, and we certainly appreciate that. It has made this trial a better trial in many ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. And I do join you, and in fact the reason why I said what I said yesterday was precisely because I thought that today's sittings would be in closed session, so I took the opportunity to make that intervention myself. I think everyone -- we ought to be grateful and thankful to everyone involved, the interpreters, the technicians. We have had problems throughout, and were it not for them, we wouldn't have arrived where we are today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The technicians today did well with this videolink. And I understood that they don't always go this smoothly but this one was extremely well done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think the only thing left is the timing of the various things. I know yesterday Mr. Ackerman's going to -- first we are going to get part of the -- part of Mr. Shoup's report today, and Mr. Ackerman presumably will let us know if Mr. Shoup is going to testify earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's one thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Secondly, of course, Your Honours, as there's going to be this -- at present this gap unless the matter we discussed earlier today is brought in next week until February the 9th, Your Honours presumably will let us know first whether you intend in this gap to call any witnesses yourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The decision will be taken either Monday or Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm grateful. And secondly, obviously at what stage, if any, the site visit is to be organised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. And that is being verified this morning by Mr. Roberts. We've cleared a lot of ground with the security, both in ex-Yugoslavia and here. Today the financial matters being attended to, and then we need to liaise with you to establish the date, and we will communicate the date to whoever needs to know the details.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The other thing is this, Ms. Korner, and I intended to raise it again with you: You mentioned earlier on that you may have some evidence in rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can -- I think we can put it this way: That we should be in a position at the latest the week after next, and maybe the end of next week to tell Your Honour whether we wish to -- because it's obviously -- we have to apply, and equally Mr. Ackerman has to be given notice of any evidence that we would wish to call in rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I thank you. But if as I mentioned to you earlier some few days ago, if it is at all possible to cooperate together with Mr. Ackerman and bring forward any evidence in rebuttal, or at least some of the evidence in rebuttal even before Mr. Shoup comes to give evidence, I think that would help us tremendously, if it is possible. I don't want to force it on you because obviously I know that there are limitations and problems that you have to encounter. If it is possible, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we certainly have that well in mind, and if it's at all possible then we will do it. I think the point that both Mr. Ackerman and I would make about this is that it doesn't really make much -- because the time that we would save, we will be doing the same thing, which is dealing with our closing briefs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So from that point of view, I think it's -- but we will certainly let Your Honours know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, when you were not here, it was Mr. Nicholls and Ms. Sutherland who were here, well we willing utilising this interval to go through several aspects of the trial and come back to you on various issues that we would like you to concentrate upon and address in your brief in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I heard that -- I was actually keeping an eye on the proceedings, as it were. But Your Honour, we would certainly welcome that and urge Your Honours to do that. As Your Honours probably know, Judge Schomburg did that in the Stakic trial, and it was of great assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's very important.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We do it in our jurisdiction, and it works. Also, the understanding is this: That when I say "Mr. Ackerman, please try to concentrate on this more than the other" it doesn't mean to say that we are already in our mind decided on anything. I want to make this clear. It's done on a -- in a spirit of cooperation between the Trial Chamber and the parties to streamline the final submissions as much as possible to what is considered at the time by the Chambers as more important or that deserves more attention anyway. And also, there may be areas that were perhaps not sufficiently addressed for one or more reasons during or in the course of the Rule 98 bis stage which will now need to be extended for sure, so we will come to those. We were identifying as we went along in our deliberations at the time, and practically that was one time when we decided that we will come back to you on several issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did on the issue of Rule 98, I made the inquiries with the senior legal officer to the Appeals Chamber as to whether we were likely to get a decision. My understanding is, although it was never actually specifically stated, that we are likely to get a decision from the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the indication that I have, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I'm working in that direction as much as I can because it's not within -- but I will not fail to emphasise the importance of having that point decided before we come to our own decision. So yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it was clear from the question that you asked of the witness, but my client has asked me to make sure to clarify that it was the Sugic brothers involved in the killing based upon records already in this case were the sons of Mica and not the sons of the cafe owner. I think that was clear, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's why I put it as the last question because earlier on he had mentioned sons of Savo and one or more of them being killed themselves, so I wanted to make that clear. Yes, that brings us to the end for the time being. We will reconvene for sure to hear the testimony of the expert which hopefully would be brought forward, advanced, if possible. Between now and then, there may be an occasion for us to reconvene if necessary. And we will let you know well in advance if that is the case. Okay. I thank you all.
